stem: A company has 40 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations with all features enabled. Employees sign in with user accounts in an Active Directory domain in the company's data center. The data center already connects to a VPC through AWS Direct Connect. The employees must use their existing Active Directory credentials to access the AWS accounts. The company does not want to run domain controllers in AWS or to keep copies of the users or passwords in AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: existing Active Directory credentials
does not want to run domain controllers in AWS
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Configure SAML 2.0 federation from an AD FS server in the data center to an IAM identity provider and IAM roles in each AWS account.
options.why: It works, but you [federate workforce users through your identity provider to specific AWS accounts](../facts/iam.md#iam-federation-with-iam-per-account-saml-or-oidc), so each account needs its own provider and roles.
options.misconception: federates each account separately when one central sign-in service exists

options.text: Create IAM users in each AWS account with a script that copies the user names from Active Directory, and require MFA for each IAM user.
options.why: Employees get new passwords, because [IAM users have long-term credentials such as passwords and access keys](../facts/iam.md#iam-users-have-long-term-credentials-roles-do-not), so the Active Directory credentials stay unused.

options.text: Use IAM Identity Center with AWS Managed Microsoft AD as the identity source, and create a trust relationship with the on-premises domain.
options.why: It runs [a highly available pair of domain controllers](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-managed-ad-dc-pair-across-azs) in AWS, but AD Connector works [without caching any information in the cloud](../facts/iam.md#iam-idc-on-premises-ad-two-options).

options.text: Use IAM Identity Center with AD Connector as the identity source, and assign permission sets to Active Directory groups for the AWS accounts.
options.why: AD Connector is a directory gateway that works [without caching any information in the cloud](../facts/iam.md#iam-idc-on-premises-ad-two-options), and permission sets give each group its access.

explanation: IAM Identity Center manages access to [multiple AWS accounts, AWS applications, and other SAML-enabled cloud applications](../facts/iam.md#iam-idc-built-on-iam-for-multi-account-access), and it [applies these permissions to the selected accounts automatically](../facts/iam.md#iam-idc-permission-sets). An on-premises domain connects through AD Connector, which works [without caching any information in the cloud](../facts/iam.md#iam-idc-on-premises-ad-two-options). Its VPC reaches the data center through a [(VPN) connection or Direct Connect](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-ad-connector-needs-vpn-or-direct-connect), and the stem gives that link. Employees keep their Active Directory credentials, and no domain controllers run in AWS.
takeaway: Employees in an on-premises Active Directory reach many accounts through IAM Identity Center with AD Connector.
twin: If the stem said "employees sign in with Okta Universal Directory" instead: connect Okta as the identity source, because IAM Identity Center supports [Microsoft Active Directory, Okta Universal Directory, Microsoft Entra ID](../facts/iam.md#iam-idc-identity-sources).
say: Use IAM Identity Center with AD Connector, so employees keep their AD passwords and no directory runs in AWS.

solvers.stem_only: Use IAM Identity Center (enabled in the Organizations management account) with AD Connector as the identity source. AD Connector is a directory proxy over the existing Direct Connect link: it forwards sign-in requests to the on-premises domain controllers, so no domain controllers run in AWS and no users or passwords are copied or cached in AWS. Assign permission sets to AD groups for the 40 accounts centrally.

stem: A company stores signed contracts as objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company manages its own keys in a hardware security module in its data center. Company policy says that the encryption keys must never be stored in AWS. Amazon S3 itself must encrypt each object at rest and decrypt it when an authorized user downloads it. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: keys must never be stored in AWS
Amazon S3 itself must encrypt each object at rest
LEAST development effort

options.text: Use SSE-KMS with a customer managed key in AWS KMS, and let the company's security team control the key policy and the key rotation.
options.why: Customer managed does not mean kept by the company: the KMS key lives in AWS KMS, [in the same Region as the bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-sse-kms-key-same-region-as-bucket).

options.text: Allow SSE-C in the bucket's default encryption settings, and send the company's key over HTTPS with every upload request and every download request.
options.why: With SSE-C, S3 performs the encryption, and [S3 never stores the encryption key](../facts/s3.md#s3-sse-c-key-never-stored-https-required), so the key stays in the company's hardware security module.

options.text: Encrypt each object in the data center with the company's key before upload, and decrypt it in the data center after download.
options.why: With client-side encryption, S3 [does not play a role in encrypting](../facts/s3.md#s3-client-side-encryption-not-exposed-to-aws) the data, but the stem asks S3 to encrypt and decrypt.
options.misconception: believes that client-side encryption counts as encryption by Amazon S3

options.text: Encrypt each object in the data center before upload, and also allow SSE-C on the bucket and send the company's key with every request.
options.why: The SSE-C layer meets the policy, but the extra client-side encryption adds code and key handling that the stem does not need.

explanation: The stem asks for encryption by Amazon S3 with a key that stays outside AWS. With SSE-C, S3 does the encryption and decryption while [you retain control of the encryption keys](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-sse-c-keys). Because [S3 never stores the encryption key](../facts/s3.md#s3-sse-c-key-never-stored-https-required), each request carries the key, and [you must use HTTPS](../facts/s3.md#s3-sse-c-key-never-stored-https-required) for those requests.
takeaway: S3 does the encryption but the key stays with the company: choose SSE-C.
twin: If the stem said "Each object must be encrypted before it leaves the data center" instead: client-side encryption, because the objects [aren't exposed to any third party, including AWS](../facts/s3.md#s3-client-side-encryption-not-exposed-to-aws).
say: S3 should do the encryption but never keep the key, so I would use SSE-C over HTTPS.

solvers.stem_only: Use server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C): the company sends its own key over HTTPS with each PUT and GET; S3 encrypts and decrypts the object but does not store the key (only a salted HMAC to validate it). Client-side encryption fails the 'S3 itself must encrypt' requirement, and SSE-KMS or SSE-S3 keep keys in AWS. Make sure the bucket does not block SSE-C requests.

stem: A company runs ten Amazon EC2 Linux instances that are not in an Auto Scaling group. Each instance has 32 GiB of memory, and the instance type supports hibernation. The instances were launched from a launch template without hibernation and with unencrypted Amazon EBS root volumes. Replacing the instances is acceptable. The company now stops the instances each night and must ensure that the memory state of each instance is kept across these nightly stops. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: launched from a launch template without hibernation
unencrypted Amazon EBS root volumes
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Turn on hibernation for the running instances, and stop them each night with the StopInstances API and its Hibernate parameter.
options.why: Hibernation is chosen [when you launch it](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-enable-only-at-launch); you [can't enable hibernation on an existing instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-enable-only-at-launch), running or stopped.

options.text: Create a launch template version with hibernation enabled and an encrypted root volume large enough for the memory, and launch replacements from it.
options.why: The root volume is an [EBS volume](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-root-volume-requirements) that [must be encrypted](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-root-volume-requirements), and 32 GiB is within the Linux limit of [150 GiB](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-ram-limits-linux-windows), so the replacements can hibernate.

options.text: Move the instances into an Auto Scaling group whose launch template enables hibernation, and hibernate the group's instances each night.
options.why: [You can't hibernate an instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-not-in-auto-scaling-group) in an Auto Scaling group; the group marks the stopped instance unhealthy and can replace it.
options.misconception: believes that instances in an Auto Scaling group can hibernate

options.text: Launch ten replacement instances one at a time in the console, and turn on hibernation and root volume encryption by hand for each one.
options.why: It works, but ten manual launches are more work and more error-prone than one launch template version that every replacement uses.

explanation: Hibernation is a launch-time setting: you [can't enable hibernation on an existing instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-enable-only-at-launch). Each replacement also needs a root volume that [must be encrypted](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-root-volume-requirements) and has room for the memory. A new launch template version holds both settings, so the ten replacements launch the same way.
takeaway: Hibernation is set at launch; to add it, launch replacements from a launch template version that enables it.
twin: If the stem said "launched with hibernation enabled and with encrypted EBS root volumes" instead: stop them with the [StopInstances API with an additional ‘Hibernate’ parameter](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-hibernate-trigger-stopinstances).
say: You can't add hibernation to a running instance, so launch replacements from a template that turns it on.

solvers.stem_only: Hibernation has to be set at launch, and the root EBS volume must be encrypted and big enough to hold the RAM, so the existing unencrypted instances cannot just be switched over. Make a new launch template version with hibernation on and an encrypted, large enough root volume, launch replacements from it, then hibernate them (stop with hibernate) each night.

docs/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/hibernating-prerequisites#You can enable hibernation support for a

solvers.flag: Neither the key nor option A says the nightly stop must change to a hibernate call, so the stem leaves open whether replacing instances alone meets the memory requirement, and A is a defensible (if higher-effort) second path.

stem: A company hosts a web application on Amazon EC2 instances. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and the target group checks the health of the application on each instance. The Auto Scaling group uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks. Sometimes the application on an instance stops answering HTTP requests, but the instance keeps running. The company must ensure that failed instances are replaced automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks
stops answering HTTP requests, but the instance keeps running
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group also acts on the results of the target group health checks.
options.why: For an instance that fails the target group check, [Elastic Load Balancing stops sending traffic to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace), and the group [replaces it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-unhealthy-replaced), with one setting and no code.

options.text: Keep the current health check settings of the Auto Scaling group, and let the group replace the instances that its health checks find unhealthy.
options.why: By default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks, and the running instance passes its EC2 status checks, so it stays in service.

options.text: Run a script on each instance that tests the application every minute and calls the Auto Scaling API to mark the instance unhealthy when a test fails.
options.why: It works, because a custom check can [mark that particular instance as](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-custom-health-check-immediate-replace) unhealthy, but the team writes code that one setting replaces.

options.text: Increase the health check grace period of the Auto Scaling group, so that the group waits longer before it checks the health of each new instance.
options.why: The grace period is the [minimum amount of time (in seconds)](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-grace-period-definition) before the group can terminate a new instance for failed health; it adds no load balancer check.
options.misconception: believes the grace period decides which health checks the group uses

explanation: The application fails while the instance keeps running, so the EC2 status checks still pass. By default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks. For the ELB health check type, [you must turn it on](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-check-must-be-turned-on); then the group marks the instance unhealthy [on its next periodic health check](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-unhealthy-replaced).
takeaway: A running instance with a failed application needs the ELB health check type on the group.
twin: If the stem said "the underlying hardware of an instance fails, and the instance fails its EC2 system status check" instead: keep the current settings, because EC2 status checks are the [default health check type](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-check-type-ec2-default).
say: The group ignores the load balancer checks until you turn them on, so I'd set the health check type to ELB.

solvers.stem_only: The application fails while the instance stays running, so EC2 status checks never see it. Add the ELB health check type to the Auto Scaling group so it replaces instances that the target group marks unhealthy.

stem: A company runs a web application on one Amazon EC2 instance. The application keeps its state in memory and cannot run as several copies. During the day the load changes often, and at peaks the CPU utilization of the instance reaches 100%. Users then see slow responses. The company expects the number of users to grow during the next year. A short stop of the instance is acceptable in a weekly maintenance window. The application must handle the growth and the daily peaks with minimal downtime outside that window. Which solution will meet these requirements?
keywords: keeps its state in memory and cannot run as several copies
at peaks the CPU utilization of the instance reaches 100%
A short stop of the instance is acceptable in a weekly maintenance window
minimal downtime

options.text: Change the instance to a larger instance type with more vCPUs and more memory, and move to a larger type again each time the load grows.
options.why: This application runs as one copy, so a larger type is the way to add vCPUs; [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required) to resize it, so do each resize in the weekly maintenance window.

options.text: Turn on detailed monitoring for the instance, so that Amazon CloudWatch publishes the CPU utilization metric every minute instead of every five minutes.
options.why: Detailed monitoring reports the metric more often, but it adds no capacity, so the single instance still runs out of CPU at the peaks.
options.misconception: believes that more frequent metrics add capacity

options.text: Run the application in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer, with a target tracking scaling policy on CPU utilization.
options.why: An Auto Scaling group runs several copies of the application, but this application keeps its state in the memory of one copy.
options.misconception: believes that every application can run as several copies behind a load balancer

options.text: Attach a second elastic network interface to the instance, so that the instance can accept twice as many user requests during the peaks.
options.why: A second network interface adds a network path, not vCPUs, so the CPU utilization of the single instance still reaches 100% at the peaks.
options.misconception: believes that a second network interface adds compute capacity

explanation: This application keeps its state in the memory of one instance and runs as one copy, so a group of several instances does not fit. More CPU and memory come from a larger instance type. To change the type, [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required), so [plan for downtime](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required) and resize in the weekly maintenance window, not during the daily peaks.
takeaway: When the application runs as one copy, move it to a larger instance type and plan a stop for each resize.
twin: If the stem said "stateless web application" instead: an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer, because adding instances is [essential for dynamic workloads with fluctuating demands](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-decision-guide-horizontal-for-fluctuating).
say: It keeps its state in one copy, so I'd move to a larger instance type and plan a short stop.

solvers.stem_only: The application keeps state in memory and cannot run as several copies, so horizontal scaling (Auto Scaling group, more instances) is ruled out. Scale vertically: resize the instance to a larger type sized for the peak, doing the stop/start in the weekly maintenance window, and repeat the resize in a later window as the user base grows.

stem: A company runs a web application on one Amazon EC2 instance. The application stores its data in files on the Amazon EBS volume of the instance and cannot run as several copies. During the day the load changes often, and at peaks the CPU utilization of the instance reaches 100%. Users then see slow responses. The company expects the number of users to grow during the next year. The application must handle the growth and the daily peaks with minimal downtime. Which solution will meet these requirements?
keywords: stores its data in files on the Amazon EBS volume of the instance and cannot run as several copies
at peaks the CPU utilization of the instance reaches 100%
minimal downtime

options.text: Change the instance to a larger instance type with more vCPUs and more memory while the instance keeps running, so that the users see no interruption.
options.why: To change the instance type, [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required), so a resize with no interruption is not possible.

options.text: Run the application in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer, with a target tracking scaling policy on CPU utilization.
options.why: Each instance that the group launches is another copy, and [data is not automatically copied](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-data-not-copied-to-new-instances) to it, so the files stay on the first instance.

options.text: Stop the instance, change it to a larger instance type with more vCPUs and more memory, and start the instance again.
options.why: It runs as one copy, so a larger type adds vCPUs and memory; [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required) to change the type, so one planned stop is the least downtime that works.

options.text: Attach a second elastic network interface to the instance, so that the instance can accept twice as many user requests during the peaks.
options.why: The option repeats the peaks of the stem, but a second network interface adds a network path, not vCPUs, so the CPU utilization still reaches 100% at the peaks.

explanation: The application keeps its files on one instance and cannot run as several copies, and [data is not automatically copied](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-data-not-copied-to-new-instances) to new instances, so a group does not fit. More vCPUs and memory come from a larger instance type. To change the type, [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required), so [plan for downtime](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required): one planned stop is the least downtime of the options that work.
takeaway: When the application runs as a single copy, move it to a larger instance type in one planned stop.
twin: If the stem said "a stateless web application" instead: an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer, because adding instances is [essential for dynamic workloads with fluctuating demands](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-decision-guide-horizontal-for-fluctuating).
say: It runs as one copy, so I'd move it once to a larger instance type and plan one short stop.

solvers.stem_only: The application keeps state in files on its EBS volume and cannot run as several copies, so horizontal scaling (Auto Scaling group, load balancer) is ruled out. Scale vertically: stop the instance, change it to a larger instance type with more vCPUs and memory, and start it again. EBS-backed instances keep their root and data volumes across a stop and start, and the instance type cannot be changed while the instance is running, so a short planned stop is the minimal downtime.

stem: A company stores customer uploads in an Amazon S3 bucket. Amazon S3 invokes an AWS Lambda function for each new object. Some uploads are malformed, and the function fails on every attempt to process them. Today, these failed events are retried and then lost. The operations team must keep a record of each failed event, with details about the failed invocation, as an object in a separate S3 bucket. The team must receive each record as soon as possible after the first failure. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: as an object in a separate S3 bucket
as soon as possible after the first failure
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Configure an on-failure destination for asynchronous invocations of the function, and choose the separate S3 bucket as the destination.
options.why: Lambda can send records of asynchronous invocations to [An Amazon S3 bucket (on failure only)](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-async-destination-targets), as a record with details about the failed invocation.

options.text: Set the maximum retry attempts in the asynchronous invocation configuration of the function to 0, so that a failed event is not retried.
options.why: The retry count can be set [between 0 and 2](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-async-retry-attempts-0-to-2); at 0, the first failure goes to the destination at once.

options.text: Configure an Amazon SQS standard queue as the dead-letter queue of the function, and read the failed events from that queue.
options.why: A dead-letter queue can be an [Amazon SQS queue or an Amazon SNS topic](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-dlq-sqs-or-sns), so no record reaches the S3 bucket.

options.text: Configure an on-failure destination for asynchronous invocations of the function, and choose an Amazon SNS FIFO topic as the destination.
options.why: A FIFO topic is an [unsupported destination type](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-destination-fifo-unsupported) for asynchronous invocation records, so no record arrives.
options.misconception: believes that any Amazon SNS topic can receive invocation records

options.text: Add error handling code to the function that writes each failed event and its error message as an object to the separate S3 bucket.
options.why: It works, but custom error code in the function is more to build and maintain than two settings in the asynchronous invocation configuration.

explanation: Amazon S3 invokes the function asynchronously. After a failure, Lambda tries [two more times](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-async-default-two-retries), and then [Lambda discards it](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-async-discard-then-destination) unless a destination keeps it. An on-failure destination can be an S3 bucket, which receives a record with details about the invocation, and a retry count of 0 sends the record after the first failure.
takeaway: Failed asynchronous events go to an on-failure destination, which can be an S3 bucket; 0 retries sends them at once.
twin: If the stem said "must keep each failed event in an Amazon SQS queue" instead: a dead-letter queue also fits, because it can be an [Amazon SQS queue or an Amazon SNS topic](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-dlq-sqs-or-sns).
say: An on-failure destination writes each failed event with its invocation details to the S3 bucket, and zero retries sends it right after the first failure.

solvers.stem_only: S3 invokes the function asynchronously. Configure an on-failure destination for asynchronous invocation with the separate S3 bucket as the destination: Lambda writes an invocation record with the event and details about the failed invocation (error, request context). To get the record right after the first failure, set the maximum retry attempts of the asynchronous invocation configuration to 0. A dead-letter queue keeps only the event with few details and is a queue, not an S3 object; custom error-handling code is more overhead and misses timeouts.

solvers.flag: A second pair, A and B (retries off, plus code in the function that writes the failed event to the S3 bucket at the first failure), is defensible because the stem does not say that failures include timeouts or runtime crashes that the function code cannot catch, so B is not clearly excluded and only the phrase 'details about the failed invocation' plus 'least operational overhead' separates it from E.

stem: A company processes clickstream records from an Amazon Kinesis data stream with an AWS Lambda function. The event source mapping uses the default settings. However, one malformed record makes the function fail, and processing of that record's shard stops for days while the other shards continue. The company wants to keep the full content of each failed record for later analysis and keep each shard moving. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: The event source mapping uses the default settings
keep the full content of each failed record
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Configure a dead-letter queue on the function, so that Lambda moves the malformed record to an Amazon SQS queue after its retries end.
options.why: A function's [dead letter queue](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-dlq-after-retries) receives asynchronous events after their retries; a stream mapping keeps failed records in its own on-failure destination.

options.text: On the event source mapping, turn on bisect batch on function error, set a retry limit, and add an Amazon S3 bucket as the on-failure destination.
options.why: [BisectBatchOnFunctionError](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-stream-bisect-batch-on-error) isolates the bad record, the retry limit ends the loop, and an [Amazon S3 bucket](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-kinesis-on-failure-destination-targets) destination receives the entire invocation record.

options.text: Raise the parallelization factor of the event source mapping, so that other concurrent batches from the same shard move past the malformed record.
options.why: More batches for each shard keep no copy of the failed record, and Lambda [stops processing additional records in a shard](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-kinesis-in-order-stops-on-error) after an error.
options.misconception: believes that more concurrent batches for each shard skip a record that keeps failing

options.text: Add code to the function that catches parse errors, writes each malformed record to an Amazon S3 bucket, and returns success for the batch.
options.why: It works, but parsing and copying code in the function is more to build and maintain than three settings on the event source mapping.

explanation: With the default settings, [failed records are retried until the record expires](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-kinesis-max-retry-attempts), so a bad record can block its shard for [up to one week](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-kinesis-bad-record-block-one-week). a separate backup account

options.why: A dump can work, but the team builds, runs and tests the export and the restore, which snapshot copies do without code.
options.misconception: moves backups with scripts when snapshot copy and sharing do it

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. In the Route 53 public hosted zone, app.example.com is an A record that holds the IP addresses of the load balancer. An engineer copied the addresses when the load balancer was created. The name receives millions of DNS queries each month. Users now report intermittent connection errors, mostly after traffic peaks. The company wants to stop the errors. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: holds the IP addresses of the load balancer
millions of DNS queries each month
intermittent connection errors, mostly after traffic peaks
MOST cost-effective

options.text: Replace the A record with a CNAME record for app.example.com whose value is the DNS name that AWS assigned to the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: It works, because the name follows the load balancer, but Route 53 [charges for CNAME queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-queries-free-cname-charged), so it costs more than an alias record.

options.text: Create a scheduled AWS Lambda function that reads the current load balancer addresses every minute and writes them into the A record for app.example.com.
options.why: The function adds cost, and resolvers keep the old addresses [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control) after each rewrite.
options.misconception: believes that rewriting the record every minute keeps every user on the current addresses

options.text: Associate Elastic IP addresses with the Application Load Balancer, and replace the values of the A record for app.example.com with those Elastic IP addresses.
options.why: Elastic IP addresses do not attach to an Application Load Balancer: in the feature table, [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) belongs to the [Network Load Balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only).

options.text: Replace the A record with an alias record of type A for app.example.com that points to the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: Route 53 follows the address changes of the load balancer for an alias record, and Amazon Route 53 [doesn't charge for alias queries to ELB](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-elb-no-query-charge) load balancers.

explanation: Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer and updates its DNS entry with a [time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds](../facts/route53.md#route53-elb-dns-entry-updated-ttl-60), so copied addresses go stale after peaks. With an alias record, [Route 53 detects changes in the resource on its own](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-follows-resource-ip-changes) and answers with the current addresses. With millions of queries a month, the query charge is what separates a CNAME record from an alias record.
takeaway: Point a name at a load balancer with an alias record: Route 53 follows its changing addresses at no query charge.
twin: If the stem said "app.example.com must point to a host name of a partner outside AWS" instead: a CNAME record, because an alias record [can only redirect queries to selected AWS resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-targets-only-selected-aws-resources).

solvers.stem_only: The ALB's IP addresses change as it scales, so a hard-coded A record goes stale. Replace it with a Route 53 alias record (type A) that targets the ALB: Route 53 follows the current addresses, and queries to alias records that point to an ELB load balancer are not charged, which beats a CNAME (charged per query) for millions of queries. An ALB cannot take Elastic IP addresses.

stem: A company serves www.example.com from three Amazon EC2 instances that have Elastic IP addresses. During a failed deployment, all three instances failed their health checks, but users still received the addresses of the failed instances. When no instance is healthy, users must see a static error page from an S3 bucket named www.example.com that is configured as a website. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

users still received the addresses of the failed instances

LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Rename the three weighted records, then create failover records for www.example.com: an alias record for the weighted records as the primary, and the S3 website as the secondary.
options.why: It works with more effort: [You can't create non-failover records](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-no-non-failover-record-same-name-type) with the name and type of failover records, so the weighted records need new names.

options.text: Lower the TTL of the three weighted records to 60 seconds, so that resolvers drop the failed addresses soon after Route 53 stops returning the unhealthy records.
options.why: When no record is healthy, Route 53 [considers all the records in the group](../facts/route53.md#route53-no-record-healthy-all-records-considered-healthy) healthy and keeps returning them, so no error page appears.

options.text: Add a fourth weighted record for www.example.com: an alias record for the S3 website endpoint with a weight of 0, and keep the three records as they are.
options.why: [All the records with nonzero weights must be unhealthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-weighted-zero-weight-caveat) before Route 53 answers with a record that has a weight of 0, so the S3 website answers only when no instance is healthy.

options.text: Add a weighted alias record for the S3 website endpoint with a weight of 0, and remove the health checks from the three records so that failed instances are left out.
options.why: When a record has no health check, Route 53 [always considers it healthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-record-without-health-check-always-healthy), so the failed instances keep their share of users.

explanation: Route 53 has [a mode of last resort](../facts/route53.md#route53-last-resort-mode-all-unhealthy-returns-answer): when every record is unhealthy, it answers with them anyway, which is why users got the failed addresses. A record with a weight of 0 waits behind the nonzero records, and the bucket already has the [same name as your domain or subdomain](../facts/route53.md#route53-s3-website-bucket-name-must-match).

So the smallest change is to add one more weighted alias record for www.example.com that points to the S3 website endpoint (the bucket name matches the record name) with weight 0, and keep the three health-checked records as they are. stem: A company plans to migrate a legacy on-premises Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The business logic of the database lives in hundreds of stored procedures that are written in PL/SQL. The company has a private network connection to AWS and a short maintenance window for the final cutover. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

stored procedures that are written in PL/SQL
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Create an Aurora read replica of the Oracle database, and promote the read replica to a standalone Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster.
options.why: Aurora makes a read replica of an RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance for [migration to Aurora PostgreSQL](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-rds-postgres-read-replica-for-migration), and an Oracle database is no such source.

stem: A company stores user session data for a web application. Every request reads or writes one session item by its session ID, and the application does not join the session data with other data. The session store holds the only copy of the session data, so the data must be stored durably. Traffic is spiky, with sudden peaks of millions of requests. Which database will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

does not join the session data
stored durably
LEAST operational overhead

options.why: The decision guide lists DynamoDB as a key-value database for [session stores or shopping carts](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-key-value-session-store), a serverless and fully managed database.

options.text: A provisioned Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster, with a sessions table on the writer and Aurora Replicas behind the reader endpoint.
options.why: It works, but the team sizes and runs a relational cluster for lookups by one key, and provisioned clusters are [suitable for steady workloads](../facts/aurora-serverless.md#aurora-serverless-provisioned-suited-to-steady-workloads), not spiky ones.

DynamoDB gives [single-digit millisecond performance at any scale](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-key-value-session-store), and AWS describes it as serverless and fully managed. Aurora fits relational work, such as [migrating or modernizing an on-premises relational workload](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-dg-use-when-relational-modernize).

B still wins on operational overhead, but the stem should state a constraint that excludes D, for example a Valkey version or the serverless deployment option, which does not support durability.

The stem gives no latency or scaling-speed number, so a careful candidate could defend Aurora Serverless v2 (option C) as fully managed, durable and load-scaling; the key rests on 'one item by key, no joins, sudden peaks of millions of requests' and on option B not naming a capacity mode.

stem: A company stores about 100 GiB of application data on an Amazon EFS Regional file system that uses Bursting throughput. The file system has used all of its burst credits, and the application slows down. The application drives a steady-state, predictable throughput close to its peak all day. The company has measured this rate over several months and expects it to stay the same. The company must restore the performance of the application. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: steady-state, predictable throughput close to its peak all day
used all of its burst credits
MOST cost-effective

options.text: Switch the file system to Elastic throughput, so that throughput scales up and down with the reads and writes of the application.
options.why: Elastic works, but AWS says to use Provisioned throughput when you [know your workload's performance requirements](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-use-when-known-needs-5-percent-or-more), and the company has measured its steady rate.
options.misconception: pays per use for a constant, high throughput

options.text: Switch the file system to Provisioned throughput, and set the provisioned level to the throughput that the application needs at its peak.
options.why: AWS names Provisioned throughput for [predictable and high levels of sustained throughput requirements](../facts/efs.md#efs-pricing-provisioned-throughput-predictable-sustained), and the level is [independent of the file system's size](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-throughput-independent-of-size).

options.text: Keep Bursting throughput, and store extra unused data in the file system to raise the baseline throughput that the file system earns.
options.why: Bursting gives [throughput that scales with the amount of storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-bursting-scales-with-storage-size-recommended-for), so the company pays to store data that nobody reads.

options.text: Create a new file system that uses the Max I/O performance mode, and copy the application data to the new file system.
options.why: Max I/O changes the performance mode, not the throughput mode, and AWS recommends [always using General Purpose performance mode](../facts/efs.md#efs-general-purpose-always-recommended-max-io-higher-latency).

explanation: The load is steady, predictable and close to its peak, and the company has measured it, so it knows the throughput that it needs. With Provisioned throughput, [you specify a level of throughput](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-throughput-independent-of-size) that the file system can drive, whatever its size or burst credits. Elastic throughput fits [spiky or unpredictable workloads](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-best-for-spiky-low-average-to-peak), which this load is not.
takeaway: Steady, known, high EFS throughput: Provisioned throughput at the level that the application needs.
twin: If the stem said "The throughput is spiky and unpredictable: the application is idle most of the day, then drives short peaks" instead: Elastic throughput, because it fits [spiky or unpredictable workloads](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-best-for-spiky-low-average-to-peak).

solvers.stem_only: Small data set with a steady, known throughput close to peak all day: Bursting cannot earn enough credits at 100 GiB, and Elastic suits spiky or unpredictable loads (it bills per amount of data transferred, which costs more for constant high use). The cost-effective fix is Provisioned throughput set to the known required rate.

solvers.flag: Option D is a second, weakly defensible answer: AWS itself says base throughput is proportionate to Standard storage size (50 KiBps per each GiB) and a Lambda troubleshooting page says to 'increase the size of the file system or use provisioned throughput' when burst credits run out. The stem gives no storage price, no throughput figure and no amount of extra data, so a reader cannot prove from the stem that padding with data costs more than Provisioned throughput; the saved AWS pages carry no price per GiB or per MiBps to settle it. Option C is still the AWS-recommended fix for a throughput-constrained Bursting file system with predictable sustained load, and D only works at a stated cost that the stem does not give.

stem: A company runs a voting application that stores each vote as an item in an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode. The partition key is the contest ID, and the application shows the running total of each contest. During a televised final, almost every vote is for one contest, at about 4,000 votes each second. Each vote item is smaller than 1 KB. Amazon CloudWatch shows that consumed write capacity is far below the provisioned write capacity of the table, but many writes are throttled. The company needs a scalable design. Which solution will BEST resolve the throttling?
keywords: almost every vote is for one contest
about 4,000 votes each second
far below the provisioned write capacity
BEST

options.text: Raise the provisioned write capacity of the table to several times the current peak, and keep the contest ID as the partition key of every vote.
options.why: The table already has spare capacity; the limit is one partition, which delivers at most [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput) whatever the table total is.

options.text: Add a random number from a fixed range to the contest ID on each write, then query each suffix and sum the results to count the votes.
options.why: Random suffixes [randomize the writes across the larger space](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-sharding-random-suffix) of keys, and a total needs one query per suffix before you [merge the results](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-sharding-read-merge).

options.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so that the table scales automatically with the burst of votes, and keep the contest ID as the partition key.
options.why: On-demand mode changes billing, not the partition ceiling of [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput), so 4,000 small votes each second on one key are still throttled.

options.text: Make a unique vote ID the partition key of every item, and count the votes of a contest with a Scan that filters on the contest ID.
options.why: It ends the throttling, but in a Scan [DynamoDB reads every item](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-reads-every-item), so each running total reads the whole table.
options.misconception: fixes the writes with a design that makes every total a full table read

explanation: Consumed capacity is far below provisioned capacity, so the table is not short of capacity; one partition key is. A partition delivers at most [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput), and [concentrated traffic that exceeds these limits](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-hot-partitions-throttle-while-others-underutilized) is throttled. Write sharding spreads one contest [across more distinct partition key values](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-few-partition-keys-spread-writes), so no single partition takes the whole burst.
takeaway: Throttling with spare table capacity means a hot partition key: spread it with a random suffix.
twin: If the stem said "consumed write capacity equals the provisioned write capacity, and the votes are spread across many contests" instead: raise the provisioned write capacity, because the table as a whole is short of capacity.
say: Spare capacity plus throttling means one hot key, so I'd shard the key with a random suffix.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution that BEST resolves the throttling.

I mark the constraints: almost every vote is for one contest at about 4,000 small writes each second, the contest ID is the partition key, consumed write capacity is far below the provisioned capacity, and the application shows a running total per contest.
Before I look at the options, I predict a change of the partition key, because throttling with spare table capacity points to one hot key, and a random suffix spreads that key.

I remove the higher provisioned capacity, because the table already has spare capacity and each partition has its own ceiling. I remove on-demand mode, because it changes billing, not the ceiling of one partition.

Between the random suffix and the unique vote ID the difference is how the totals are read; the stem needs a running total per contest, so a Scan of the whole table for each total is the weaker design.
Check: the random suffix spreads the writes, a total needs one query per suffix, and every constraint is met. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.flag: Minor stem gap: the stem never says the table has a sort key (for example a vote ID), yet with contest ID as the only key each vote would overwrite the previous item; stating the sort key would remove the doubt, and it does not change the key.
solvers.stem_only: This is a hot partition key: one contest ID takes almost all writes, so a single partition hits its per-partition write limit while table-level capacity is unused. Fix the key design with write sharding: append a random suffix from a fixed range to the contest ID so writes spread over many partitions, then read all suffixes and sum for the total.

solvers.flag: The stem does not say whether the table has a sort key, and a careful candidate could defend C (on-demand mode, which can also isolate hot items by splitting partitions) if the votes have a sort key; adding a line that the single contest ID value receives all traffic and that a single partition key value is capped would remove the doubt.

stem: A company runs a mission-critical order API on an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode. Every night, a report job scans the whole table with strongly consistent reads and a filter expression that keeps only orders with the status OPEN. A small share of the orders are open at any time, and the report can use data that is a few minutes old. The company wants no new tables or functions to operate. During the job, the order API is throttled. Which TWO actions will reduce the read capacity that the job consumes in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: a filter expression that keeps only orders with the status OPEN
A small share of the orders are open
the report can use data that is a few minutes old
MOST cost-effective

options.text: Make the filter expression of the scan more selective, so that the scan returns fewer order items to the report job.
options.why: A filter runs after the read, so the scan [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity) with or without it.

options.text: Add an attribute that only open orders carry, create a global secondary index on that attribute, and change the job to query the index.
options.why: The index [only tracks data items](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-only-items-with-key-attributes) that carry its key, so it is [faster and less expensive to query that index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-sparse-index-faster-cheaper-than-scan).

options.text: Add a projection expression to the scan, so that DynamoDB returns only the few attributes that the report needs.
options.why: Read capacity depends on [the number of items and the size](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-capacity-by-items-read-not-returned) of the items that the scan reads, not on the data it returns.

options.text: Change the scan of the report job from strongly consistent reads to eventually consistent reads, and keep the same filter expression.
options.why: Eventually consistent reads cost [half the cost of strongly consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost), and the report accepts data that is minutes old.

options.text: Copy each open order into a second DynamoDB table with a Lambda function on the stream of the table, and scan the second table.
options.why: It adds a second table and a Lambda function, which the company does not want to operate, and it also pays for every copied write.
options.misconception: A copy that custom code keeps in sync is the cheapest way to isolate a report.

explanation: A filter does not help, because the scan still [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity). A sparse global secondary index [only tracks data items](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-only-items-with-key-attributes) that carry its key attribute, so the job reads far fewer items. Eventually consistent reads then cost [half the cost of strongly consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost).
takeaway: Filters and projections do not lower scan capacity; a sparse index and eventually consistent reads do.
twin: If the stem said "the report lists every order, open or closed" instead: the sparse index stops helping, because the job reads every item, and eventually consistent reads still help.
say: To cut the read capacity of a report, I query a sparse index and use eventually consistent reads; a filter saves nothing.

solvers.stem_only: A scan is charged for every item it reads before filters and projections apply, so filters and projections do not help. Reduce consumed capacity by (1) switching the scan to eventually consistent reads, which costs half as much, since stale data is acceptable, and (2) replacing the full scan with a query on a sparse global secondary index keyed on an attribute that only open orders carry.

stem: An online store keeps its orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode, and a mission-critical checkout API reads and writes items in the table. Two other workloads use most of the read capacity. A status page calls GetItem with strongly consistent reads for single orders, and the page can show data that is a few seconds old. Each night, a report job runs a Scan of the whole table with a filter expression that returns the orders whose status is OPEN; few orders are open at any time. The reads of the checkout API are throttled. Which TWO actions will reduce the read capacity that the two workloads consume with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: can show data that is a few seconds old
returns the orders whose status is OPEN
few orders are open at any time
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Make the filter expression of the nightly Scan more selective, so that the Scan returns fewer order items to the report job.
options.why: A filter runs after the read, so the Scan still [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity) as without it.

options.text: Add an attribute that only open orders carry, create a global secondary index on that attribute, and change the report job to query that index.
options.why: The index [only tracks data items](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-only-items-with-key-attributes) that carry its key, so it is [faster and less expensive to query that index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-sparse-index-faster-cheaper-than-scan), and [DynamoDB maintains indexes automatically](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-indexes-maintained-automatically).

options.text: Create a DAX cluster, and send the strongly consistent GetItem calls of the status page through the DAX client so that DAX serves them from memory.
options.why: [DAX passes strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions) without a cache, so the table still serves every one of these reads.

options.text: Change the GetItem calls of the status page from strongly consistent reads to eventually consistent reads by setting ConsistentRead to false.
options.why: [Eventually consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost) cost [half the cost of strongly consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost), and the page accepts older data.

options.text: Copy each open order into a second table with a Lambda function on the stream of the table, and change the report job to scan the second table.
options.why: It also lowers the reads of the table, but the company must then run copy code and a second table, while [DynamoDB maintains indexes automatically](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-indexes-maintained-automatically).
options.misconception: A copy that custom code keeps in sync is the simplest way to take a report off a table.

explanation: Each workload needs its own fix. The report filters after it reads, so it [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity) as an unfiltered Scan; a sparse index [only tracks data items](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-only-items-with-key-attributes) that carry its key attribute. A synced copy table also works, but [DynamoDB maintains indexes automatically](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-indexes-maintained-automatically). The status page accepts older data, and [Eventually consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost) cost half as much.
takeaway: Filters and DAX do not cut these reads; a sparse index and eventually consistent reads do.
twin: If the stem said "the status page must show the latest write" instead: keep its strongly consistent reads, because they return the [most up-to-date data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-consistentread-parameter).
say: For the report I query a sparse index, and for the status page I use eventually consistent reads.

solvers.stem_only: Status page: switch its GetItem calls to eventually consistent reads, which cost half the read capacity of strongly consistent reads and fit data a few seconds old. Nightly report: a filter expression is applied after the read, so the Scan still consumes capacity for the whole table; use a sparse global secondary index on an attribute that only open orders carry and query the index (its reads use the index capacity, not the table's).

solvers.flag: Option D (copy open orders to a second table with a stream-triggered Lambda) also removes the scan reads from the main table, so only the unmeasured claim that a sparse GSI has less operational overhead separates E from D.

stem: A company uses an AWS Lambda function to process messages from an Amazon SQS standard queue. The event source mapping uses a batch size of 10, and the queue has a redrive policy with a dead-letter queue. When one message in a batch is malformed, the function returns an error for the whole batch. The other nine messages are processed again and again, and at last all ten messages move to the dead-letter queue. Which solution will retry only the malformed message in the MOST operationally efficient way?
keywords: returns an error for the whole batch
retry only the malformed message
MOST operationally efficient

options.text: Change the function to delete each message that it processes without error from the queue, and then return an error for the batch when one message fails.
options.why: It works, but the company writes and runs delete calls for each good message, which the built-in partial batch response replaces with one returned list of failed IDs.
options.misconception: Deleting the good messages in the function code is the efficient way to keep them from a retry.

options.text: Configure an on-failure destination for the function that sends the records of failed invocations to a second SQS queue for review.
options.why: For a queue, the [visibility timeout and redrive policy](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-queue-esm-retry-set-on-queue) on the source queue decide retries and failed messages, not a setting of the function.

options.text: Lower the visibility timeout of the queue so that a failed batch returns to the function sooner and the good messages finish faster.
options.why: A shorter timeout returns the whole batch sooner; it does not separate the malformed message from the nine good ones.

options.text: Turn on ReportBatchItemFailures in the event source mapping, and change the function to return the IDs of the messages that failed.
options.why: With [ReportBatchItemFailures](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sqs-partial-batch-response), Lambda can [make only the failed messages visible again](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sqs-partial-batch-response), so the good messages are not retried.

explanation: A function error returns the whole batch to the queue, so the nine good messages come back with the bad one. With a [partial batch response](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sqs-partial-batch-response), the function reports which messages failed. The good messages are not processed again, and the queue's redrive policy moves the malformed message to the dead-letter queue.
takeaway: For Lambda with SQS, turn on ReportBatchItemFailures so that one bad message does not send a whole batch back.
twin: If the stem said "without any change to the function code" instead: set the batch size of the event source mapping to 1, because a partial batch response needs the function to return the failed message IDs.
say: I'd turn on a partial batch response, so the function reports the one failed message and the rest are done.

solvers.stem_only: Turn on partial batch responses: set FunctionResponseTypes to ReportBatchItemFailures on the SQS event source mapping and have the function return batchItemFailures with the message IDs that failed. Lambda then deletes the successful messages and only the malformed one returns to the queue and, after maxReceiveCount, moves to the dead-letter queue.
